newsitem.title: INDIA: Record candidates in first phase of Kashmir polls.
newsitem.headline: Record candidates in first phase of Kashmir polls.

text.p: A record number of candidates will contest the initial phase of local assembly elections being held in Jammu and Kashmir for the first time since a separatist rebellion broke out in 1990.
Polling will be held in 26 of the state's 87 constituencies on Saturday.
Voting in the remaining constituencies will be spread over three days -- September 16, 21 and 30 -- to allow polling officials and thousands of security forces to move between regions.
The elections are the first to the state assembly since 1987. The last assembly was dissolved in February 1990, shortly after the separatist insurgency erupted.
The state has been under New Delhi's direct rule since then.

The Himalayan state which borders Pakistan to the west and China to the north and east held parliamentary polls in May as part of general elections which brought Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda to power.
In those elections, Jammu and Kashmir voters chose six representatives to sit in the lower house of parliament, the Lok Sabha, in New Delhi.
Voting on Saturday will be conducted in parts of the state's three regions -- the mostly Moslem Kashmir Valley to the north, Hindu majority Jammu to the south and Buddhist Ladakh to the east.
Voting will be held on September 16 in the state's winter capital Jammu and on September 21 in the summer capital Srinagar.
A record 142 candidates, up from 116 in 1987 and 122 in 1983, are contesting the 26 seats. All major parties, both regional and national, with organisations in the state are participating.
Some 1.3 million voters, including more than 610,000 women, are eligible to vote on Saturday. However, there are only two women candidates.
The state's largest pro-India party, the National Conference, is tipped to win the most seats although some polls showed it short of an outright majority.

The All Parties Hurriyat (Freedom) Conference, which includes 30 separatist groups, has urged voters to boycott the polls. Hurriyat member groups favour either merger with neighbouring Pakistan or independence.

On paper the Jammu and Kashmir assembly has a total of 111 seats. However, 24 constituencies fall within the one third of Kashmir which Pakistan governs. Earlier this year, elections were held in Pakistan-controlled Kashmir.

Pakistan, which has staked a claim over all of Kashmir, wants an internationally supervised plebiscite of Kashmiris to determine the status of the region. India wants to resume high-level bilateral talks, which were last held in early 1994, to settle the issue.
